case_name: Smt. Pushpa v Union of India and Others
facts: This petition u/art. 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus is filed by Smt. Pushpa describing herself as the wife of Shri Pala Singh, son of Shri Sarwan who has been detained by an order made by the third respondent, Chief Secretary, Delhi Administration, on January 27, 1979 u/s. 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 ('COFEPOSA' for short).
The detenu was arrested on December 31, 1978 and was produced before the Magistrate on January 2, 1979 when he was remanded to custody.
While he was in Jain custody, a detention order dated January 27, 1979 made by the third respondent, Chief Secretary to Delhi Administration was served upon him.
The grounds of detention signed by the detaining authority were also served upon him on January 30, 1979.

A request for copies appears not to have been complied with till February 23, 1979 when learned Advocate Shri Harjinder Singh submitted a representation as contemplated by cl. (5) of Art. 22 of the Constitution on behalf of the detenu.
issues: Validity of the detention of the detenu has been questioned inter alia on the following grounds :
Whether the Chief Secretary was competent to reject the representations made by the detenu.

Whether the order confirming the detention of the detenu after obtaining the opinion of the Advisory Board is invalid as the same has been confirmed beyond the prescribed period of three months, the delay being of three days.

Whether the constitutional right of the detenu to make a representation was seriously undermined because of the inordinate delay in complying with the request of the detenu for copies of the documents from February 9 to March 9, 1979.
petitioner_arguments: The first contention is that the representation made by or on behalf of detenu on February 23, 1979 and March 27, 1979 were rejected by the Chief Secretary who had passed the detention order though he was not competent to reject the representations.

The obligation to furnish grounds for preventive detention and the constitutional right conferred on the detenu to make a representation on receipt of the grounds of detention when read in the context of S. 11 would spell out a scheme that the representation, if and when made, may furnish such information to the detaining authority which may necessitate revocation of the detention order.
The importance of the constitutional right to make a representation and the corresponding duty to consider the representation cannot be underestimated and should not be whittled down.
respondent_arguments: In fact the representation were addressed to the third respondent and, therefore, he was competent to deal with the same;
No representation was made by the detenu to the appropriate Government.

The power to detain is conferred not only upon the State Government but any officer of the State Government not below the rank of a Secretary to the Government specially empowered for the purpose of S. 3 by that Government.
court_reasoning: This Court in Jayanarayan Sukul v. State of West Bengal (1969 Indlaw SC 445, 1970 Indlaw SC 354, ), enunciated the following four principles to be followed in regard to the representation of a detenu.

The consideration of the representation of the detenu by the appropriate authority is entirely independent of any action by the Advisory Board including the consideration of the representation of the detenu by the Advisory Board.
There should not be any delay in the matter of consideration.
holding: Therefore, the importance of the constitutional right to make a representation and the corresponding duty to consider the representation cannot be underestimated and should not be whittled down.

It is too late in the day to minimise the importance of a representation that a detenu is entitled to make and the obligation of the appropriate Government to examine the same, applying mind to the points raised therein before a further action is taken in the process of deprivation of liberty of a citizen.
cases_cited: Smt. Pushpa v Union of India
This view was reaffirmed in Sk. Sekawat v. State of W
